extracted.intended_audience: travellers, art historians, architects, patrons of art, and conservators interested in Venetian sculpture, painting, and architectural detail
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for judging Venetian Gothic sculpture, architectural capitals, paintings, conservation/restoration practices, and related craft (including practical notes on gondola handling and pulpit placement). Aimed at travellers, patrons, and students of art/architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital design (upper arcade)
rubrics_metrics.description: Their design is formed, as in the lower series, of eight leaves, thrown into volutes at the angles, and sustaining figures at the flanks; these figures have no inscriptions and, though evidently not without meaning, cannot be interpreted without more knowledge of ancient symbolism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate capitals by their leaf-forms, volute treatment, and attendant figures; note that symbolic meaning may require specialist knowledge. Look for the eight-leaf composition and volute-angling as markers of the series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity versus restoration in capitals
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the capitals toward the Sea appear to have been restored, and to be rude copies of the ancient ones; others, though apparently original, have been somewhat carelessly wrought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish genuine, carefully treated capitals (higher merit) from restored or crude copies (lower merit). Inspect workmanship closely — restored pieces often lack the refinement of originals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graceful composition for distant effect
rubrics_metrics.description: As examples of graceful composition in massy capitals meant for hard service and distant effect, these are among the finest things I know in Gothic art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging capitals intended to be seen from a distance, prioritize strong, architectural massing and compositional grace that sustain distant viewing rather than fine near-detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iconographic coherence (Four Winds capital)
rubrics_metrics.description: The capital above the fig-tree is remarkable for its sculptures of the four winds; each on the side turned towards the wind represented (Levante east, crowned Hotro south, Ponente west, Tramontana north).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess figurative capitals for coherence between form and intended meaning — e.g., directional orientation and attributes corresponding to the winds. Use such examples as instructive models of integrated iconography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of engraving/reproduction for early sculpture
rubrics_metrics.description: All the bluntness and coarseness of feeling in the workmanship of fig. 14 have disappeared on this small scale, and all the subtle refinements in the broad masses of fig. 12 have vanished. They could not, indeed, be rendered in line engraving, unless by the hand of Albert Durer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious using line engravings or small reproductions to judge early sculpture; many formal qualities (broad masses, subtle refinements) are lost. Prefer casts or in-person inspection for accurate assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of superior leafage sculpture
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect, pure, unlaboured naturalism; the freshness, elasticity, and softness of their leafage, united with the most noble symmetry and severe reserve — no running to waste, no loose or experimental lines, no extravagance, and no weakness. Their design is always sternly architectural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge leafage by combined naturalism and architectural restraint: look for freshness, elasticity, softness, noble symmetry, and disciplined restraint (no wasted or loose lines). Valuate severity and structural suitability for stone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodization: central Gothic peak circa 1350
rubrics_metrics.description: This early sculpture of the Ducal Palace ... represents the state of Gothic work in Venice at its central and proudest period, i.e. circa 1350. After this time, all is decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stylistic markers of the mid-14th century as indicators of the high point of Venetian Gothic; subsequent works should be scrutinized for signs of decline or Renaissance influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interior renewals vs original character
rubrics_metrics.description: All vestige of the earlier modes of decoration [in the interior] was destroyed by the fires; the severe and religious work of Guariento and Bellini has been replaced by the wildness of Tintoret and the luxury of Veronese. In this case, though widely different in temper, the art of the renewal was at least intellectually as great as that which had perished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging later decorative schemes, distinguish temperament (severe vs wild/luxurious) from intellectual/artistic merit; replacement does not automatically imply inferiority — assess on artistic and intellectual merits, not just fidelity to original.

rubrics_metrics.name: How reputations of pictures form
rubrics_metrics.description: The reputation of certain works is raised, partly by accident, partly by the just testimony of artists, partly by the various and generally bad taste of the public (no picture... has ever, in modern times, attained popularity ... without having some exceedingly bad qualities mingled with its good ones).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of popular reputation as an absolute quality marker. Consider provenance, artists' testimony, and possible accidental elevation when estimating a work's intrinsic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market/patron criteria for valued pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: The pictures that are most valued are for the most part those by masters of established renown, which are highly or neatly finished, and of a size small enough to admit of their being placed in galleries or saloons, so as to be made subjects of ostentation, and to be easily seen by a crowd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that market/patron preferences (small, highly finished, easily displayed works) bias which works are preserved and valued; account for this when assessing collections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleaning and restoring as destructive practices
rubrics_metrics.description: For the support of the fame and value of such pictures, little more is necessary than that they should be kept bright, partly by cleaning, which is incipient destruction, and partly by what is called 'restoring,' that is, painting over, which is of course total destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat cleaning and repainting as potentially destructive interventions. Prioritize conservation methods that preserve original material; regard over-cleaning and repainting as anti-patterns that irreversibly damage authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of spontaneous, large-scale works
rubrics_metrics.description: The most precious works of any noble painter are usually those which have been done quickly, and in the heat of the first thought, on a large scale, for places where there was little likelihood of their being well seen, or for patrons from whom there was little prospect of rich remuneration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating paintings, give weight to freshness, spontaneity, scale and original context (murals, chapels, etc.); such works often retain more of a master's true quality and are less likely to have been 'restored' away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect as accidental preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Works thus executed are of course despised ... They are, therefore, almost universally neglected, whitewashed by custodes, shot at by soldiers ... but, which is an advantage more than counterbalancing all this evil, they are not often 'restored.' What is left of them, however fragmentary ... is almost always the real thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that institutional neglect can paradoxically preserve authenticity by preventing destructive 'restoration.' When assessing fragments or ruinous works, favor original material over later overpainting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional tendencies in conservation spending
rubrics_metrics.description: It constantly happens, that public bodies who will not pay five pounds to preserve a picture, will pay fifty to repaint it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that institutional incentives often favor conspicuous 'restoration' over preventive conservation; advocate for funding priorities that favor preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gondola management and commands (practical skill rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: A gondola is in general rowed only by one man ... the forcola is of different forms ... the forward stroke would turn the boat left unless corrected by the return stroke; to turn left use forward impulse without return stroke ('Premi'); to turn right bring the plunged oar up ('Stali'); warning cry conventions dictate yielding the outside to the warning boat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess gondolier skill by: correct forcola selection and use; mastery of forward vs return stroke to control heading; correct use and response to cries ('Premi', 'Stali', 'Sciar'); ability to check lee-way with foot against wall when turning in narrow canals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste and position of modern pulpits
rubrics_metrics.description: The peculiar pompousness of the furniture of the pulpits ... without grace or meaning, dependent merely on certain applications of upholstery ... I do not understand how our congregations can endure the aspect of the wooden sounding-board attached only by one point ... The question of the position of the pulpit presents a more disputable ground of discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate pulpit design and placement for appropriateness to church architecture and liturgical function: avoid pompous, unrelated upholstery; consider historical/primitive arrangements (eastern extremity) and the evidence that lateral pulpits are later additions.
